shots.name: 1 · Wide set
shots.purpose: exterior: the car alone on the night highway, tracked from behind
shots.why: The establishing frame answers 'where are we' so every later close-up can be placed in space. Following from behind makes us move with the character without seeing what they feel. The windshield two-shot holds both people and the world rushing at them; matched window singles give the argument its emphasis; the hands insert carries what neither says, and the back-seat view after an exterior reset shows the road they still have to share.
alternatives: Avoid cutting straight from the windshield two-shot to the back-seat view: the driver jumps from screen-left to screen-right and the cut feels like a mistake.
Hold it longer than feels comfortable if the scene needs more weight; wides earn their duration.

shots.name: 3 · Medium close-up A
shots.purpose: driver single from the passenger-side position
shots.why: A medium close-up is the dialogue workhorse: the face dominates but gesture still reads. Seated eye height keeps us at the table with them, as an equal guest. Rule: keep the driver on the same screen side in every interior setup (driver screen-left through the windshield means passenger screen-right) and do not mix windshield and back-seat setups without a cutaway, because front and back views flip left and right; the audience will feel the occupants swapped seats.
alternatives: Avoid wide lenses tight on faces from the dashboard: the cramped distance distorts faces; keep wide lenses for the two-shot and use the opposite seat or window positions for singles.
For more pressure, make it a slow push-in that lands one size tighter.
